## Why circular motion is special
An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating because its direction changes continuously. Velocity is a vector: change the direction, and you change the velocity. The acceleration that turns the velocity toward the center is called centripetal acceleration; it never changes speed, only direction.
The net force that produces centripetal acceleration is the centripetal force, and it must be supplied by something real: tension in a string, friction on a tire, or gravity on a satellite. For uniform circular motion (constant speed), the key formulas are: centripetal acceleration a = v²/r, centripetal force F = m v²/r, and speed from the period T: v = 2πr/T. The acceleration vector always points from the object toward the center, perpendicular to the velocity.

## Key formulas for uniform circular motion
In uniform circular motion, an object moves at constant speed but still accelerates because its direction changes continuously. This acceleration, called centripetal acceleration, always points toward the center of the circle and never changes the speed, only the direction.
The net force causing this acceleration is the centripetal force, which must be supplied by something real, such as tension in a string, friction on a tire, or gravity on a satellite.
The key formulas are: centripetal acceleration a = v²/r, centripetal force F = m v²/r, and speed from the period T (time for one full circle) v = 2πr/T. Units: v in m/s, r in m, a in m/s², F in N, T in s.
Key: The net force that produces it is the centripetal force, and it must be supplied by something real: tension in a string, friction on a tire, or gravity on a satellite.
Key: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating, because its direction changes continuously.
Key: Speed from the period T (time for one full circle): v = 2πr / T

Q: What is the direction of the centripetal acceleration vector? A: toward the center. The passage says the acceleration vector always points from the object toward the center of the circle.
Q: A satellite orbits Earth. What supplies the centripetal force? A: Gravity. The passage lists gravity on a satellite as a real source of centripetal force.

## Worked example: car on a flat curve
When a car rounds an unbanked (flat) curve, the only horizontal force that can change its direction is friction between the tires and the road. This friction must point toward the center of the curve to provide the centripetal force needed for circular motion.
In the worked example, a 1200 kg car at 20 m/s on a 50 m radius curve has centripetal acceleration a = v²/r = 8.0 m/s². The required force is F = ma = 9600 N (about 9.6 kN).
If the maximum available friction is less than this required force (e.g., on ice or with worn tires), the car cannot turn sharply enough. It skids outward—not because an outward force pushes it, but because the centripetal force is missing, so the car continues in a straight line (Newton's first law).

Key: Required force = m * (v²/r).
Key: If friction is insufficient, the car skids outward due to lack of centripetal force, not an outward force.

## Worked example: geostationary satellite
A geostationary satellite orbits Earth in a circle with a period of 24 hours, matching Earth's rotation. Its orbital speed is found from the circumference of the orbit divided by the period: v = 2πr / T. For a radius of 4.23 × 10⁷ m and T = 86,400 s, the speed is about 3.1 km/s.
The centripetal acceleration needed to keep it in circular motion is a = v² / r. Plugging in the values gives about 0.22 m/s². This acceleration is provided entirely by Earth's gravity, which pulls the satellite toward the center of the orbit.
The satellite is in free fall—it is continuously falling toward Earth but moving sideways fast enough that it keeps missing. It is not floating without forces; gravity is acting on it, providing the centripetal force that bends its path into a circle.

Centripetal force is not a new kind of force; it is the name for whatever real force (tension, friction, gravity, a normal force) points toward the center. Never draw a 'centripetal force' arrow on a free-body diagram in addition to the actual forces — identify which actual force plays that role.

## Scope and Definitions
This law applies to all residential lease agreements made within the Republic of Ostrava. Key terms are defined: a Tenant is any natural person who occupies a dwelling under a written lease; a Landlord is the legal holder of title or the authorized manager of the premises; and the Regulatory Office is the Office of Tenancy Regulation established under Article 12.
The law sets a minimum lease term of 120 calendar days, unless both parties agree in writing to a shorter term, which cannot be less than 30 days. Any lease shorter than 30 days is void from the start.
Rent can be increased at most once every 12 months. The increase cannot exceed 5% of the prevailing rent, unless the Landlord gets prior written approval from the Housing Arbitration Bureau showing that capital improvements exceeding 15% of the property's assessed value have been completed. This provision will be on the upcoming assessment.
A security deposit cannot exceed two months' rent. It must be held in an escrow account by the Ministry of Urban Dwelling and returned within 45 days after the lease ends, minus lawful deductions for damage beyond normal wear.
The Landlord must keep structural elements, plumbing, heating, and electrical systems in habitable condition. The Tenant must keep the interior clean and promptly notify the Landlord of any defect. If the Landlord fails to fix a reported defect within 14 days, the Tenant can reduce rent by up to 10% per month until it is fixed.
Either party can end a periodic tenancy by giving written notice at least 60 days before the intended termination date.

## Penicillins
Penicillins are beta-lactam antibiotics. Penicillin G has a narrow spectrum (G+ and some G-), while amoxicillin is broader and covers some H. influenzae. Flucloxacillin targets MSSA, and co-amoxiclav adds beta-lactamase coverage.
Dosing and renal adjustment: Penicillin G is IV 2-4 MU q4-6h; amoxicillin 500 mg-1 g PO/IV q8h; flucloxacillin 500 mg-1 g PO q6h; co-amoxiclav 625 mg PO q12h. For renal impairment (CrCl<30), halve penicillin G, adjust amoxicillin by 25-50%, reduce flucloxacillin by 50%, and adjust co-amoxiclav dose and interval.
Contraindications: anaphylaxis to penicillins (for penicillin G), severe allergic disease (amoxicillin), hepatic impairment (flucloxacillin), hepatic dysfunction (co-amoxiclav). Cephalosporins like cefadroxil/cefalexin have ~10% cross-reactivity with penicillin.
Exam traps: Penicillin is the drug of choice for syphilis, but use doxycycline if allergic. Amoxicillin alone does not cover MRSA. Flucloxacillin is not for G- infections. Co-amoxiclav is not safe in penicillin allergy. First-generation cephalosporins do not cover Pseudomonas.

## Cephalosporins
Cephalosporins are beta-lactam antibiotics grouped by generation. First-generation drugs like cefalexin cover MSSA, strep, and some E. coli, but not Pseudomonas. Second-generation cefuroxime adds H. influenzae and Moraxella, but it is not anti-pseudomonal; you need a third- or fourth-generation agent for Pseudomonas.
Third-generation ceftriaxone covers good Gram-negative organisms including Neisseria and H. influenzae, and needs minimal renal adjustment. However, avoid it in hyperbilirubinemia because it can displace bilirubin. Ceftazidime is a third-generation drug with anti-pseudomonal activity, but its anaerobic coverage is limited. Fourth-generation cefepime is broad and anti-pseudomonal, but it requires dose reduction and interval extension if CrCl is below 50 mL/min; it is not safe in renal failure without adjustment.
Key exam traps: Penicillin is the drug of choice for syphilis, but use doxycycline if allergic. Amoxicillin alone does not cover MRSA; it needs an add-on. Second-generation drugs are not anti-pseudomonal. Ceftriaxone is risky in hyperbilirubinemia. Ceftazidime has limited anaerobic coverage. Cefepime needs renal adjustment. ## Carbapenems and Monobactam
Carbapenems (meropenem, imipenem, ertapenem) are broad-spectrum beta-lactams, but none cover MRSA. For MRSA, you need a glycopeptide (e.g., vancomycin) or an oxazolidinone (e.g., linezolid). Meropenem and imipenem cover Pseudomonas, but ertapenem does not. Imipenem is not first-line for community pneumonia; macrolides or doxycycline are preferred.
Aztreonam is a monobactam that covers only aerobic Gram-negative bacteria. It has no activity against Gram-positives, so it is ineffective for Gram-positive infections even in penicillin-allergic patients. It does not cross-react with penicillins or cephalosporins.
Among fluoroquinolones, ciprofloxacin is the anti-pseudomonal agent, not levofloxacin. Levofloxacin has broader atypical coverage but lacks reliable anti-pseudomonal activity. Ciprofloxacin has limited activity against atypicals like Mycoplasma and Chlamydia, so add a macrolide when treating atypical pneumonia.

## Fluoroquinolones
Fluoroquinolones include ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and moxifloxacin. Ciprofloxacin is the go-to for Pseudomonas, but it has limited activity against atypicals like Mycoplasma and Chlamydia, so add a macrolide. Levofloxacin covers atypicals well but is NOT anti-Pseudomonal. Moxifloxacin is potent against streptococci, atypicals, and anaerobes, but it is NOT for MRSA. Ertapenem does not cover MRSA, and aztreonam is ineffective against Gram-positives, so it cannot treat Gram-positive infections in penicillin-allergic patients.
Dosing: ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO/IV q12h; moxifloxacin 400 mg PO/IV q24h. Renal handling: moxifloxacin is largely unchanged, use caution if CrCl<30; ciprofloxacin halve dose if CrCl<30, avoid if <15. All carry risks of tendon rupture and QT prolongation.

## Macrolides and Lincosamides
Macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin) and clindamycin are antibiotics with similar spectra: Gram-positive bacteria, some Gram-negatives, and atypicals (Legionella, Mycoplasma). They are generally safe in renal failure because they are metabolized by the liver, so no dose adjustment is needed. However, watch for side effects like GI upset, QTc prolongation, and CYP3A4 interactions.
Erythromycin is dosed 250–500 mg PO q6h (or 500 mg q8h). Clarithromycin is 250–500 mg PO q12h and is a stronger CYP3A4 inhibitor. Azithromycin is 500 mg PO day 1 then 250 mg PO q24h for 4 days, with excellent atypical coverage and good tissue penetration.

Clindamycin is not first-line for uncomplicated strep throat; penicillin is preferred. Also, azithromycin does not cover MRSA, and doxycycline does not cover Pseudomonas.
Clindamycin is dosed 300–600 mg PO/IV q6h and covers Gram-positives (including MRSA at higher doses), anaerobes, and protozoa. Its major concern is C. difficile colitis. Doxycycline (a tetracycline) is dosed 100 mg PO/IV q12h and covers Rickettsia, Chlamydia, and spirochetes, but avoid if CrCl <30 due to accumulation.

They do NOT cover Pseudomonas. Doxycycline is given 100 mg PO/IV q12h; minocycline 100 mg PO q12h, with minocycline preferred for acne and causing less photosensitivity. Both are avoided in pregnancy (discolors teeth), children under 8, and when CrCl < 30 (accumulation).
Macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin) cover Gram-positives, some Gram-negatives, and atypicals (Legionella, Mycoplasma). Erythromycin is dosed 250–500 mg PO q6h (or 500 mg q8h); clarithromycin 250–500 mg PO q12h; azithromycin 500 mg PO day 1 then 250 mg PO q24h for 4 days. All are safe in renal failure (no adjustment), but watch for GI upset, QTc prolongation, and CYP3A4 interactions (strongest with clarithromycin). Clarithromycin alone does NOT treat H. pylori; it needs PPI plus amoxicillin or metronidazole. Azithromycin does NOT cover MRSA.
Clindamycin (300–600 mg PO/IV q6h) covers Gram-positives (including MRSA at higher doses), anaerobes, and protozoa. It is NOT first-line for uncomplicated strep throat—penicillin is preferred. It carries a risk of C. difficile colitis.
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) are for Gram-negative aerobes (e.g., Pseudomonas, Enterobacteriaceae). Gentamicin is dosed 5 mg/kg IV q24h (or extended-interval 5–7 mg/kg with trough monitoring); tobramycin is similar and anti-Pseudomonal; amikacin 15 mg/kg IV q24h for multi-drug resistant Gram-negatives. They require major dose reduction in renal failure and therapeutic drug monitoring; they are ototoxic and nephrotoxic. Gentamicin cannot be given without monitoring in stable CKD. Tobramycin is NOT effective against anaerobes. Amikacin is NOT safe in anuric patients—it requires dialysis removal.
Vancomycin (15–20 mg/kg IV q12h, adjusted to trough 15–20 µg/mL for serious infections) covers Gram-positives including MRSA and susceptible VRE. It does NOT cover Gram-negatives. It can cause nephrotoxicity and red man syndrome with rapid infusion.

## Tetracyclines
Tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline) are broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative, atypical bacteria (Rickettsia, Chlamydia), and spirochetes. They do NOT cover Pseudomonas. Doxycycline is given 100 mg PO/IV q12h; minocycline 100 mg PO q12h, with minocycline preferred for acne and causing less photosensitivity. Both are avoided in pregnancy (discolors teeth), children under 8, and when CrCl < 30 (accumulation).
Macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin) cover Gram-positives, some Gram-negatives, and atypicals (Legionella, Mycoplasma). Erythromycin is dosed 250–500 mg PO q6h (or 500 mg q8h); clarithromycin 250–500 mg PO q12h; azithromycin 500 mg PO day 1 then 250 mg PO q24h for 4 days. All are safe in renal failure (no adjustment), but watch for GI upset, QTc prolongation, and CYP3A4 interactions (strongest with clarithromycin). Clarithromycin alone does NOT treat H. pylori; it needs PPI plus amoxicillin or metronidazole. Azithromycin does NOT cover MRSA.
Clindamycin (300–600 mg PO/IV q6h) covers Gram-positives (including MRSA at higher doses), anaerobes, and protozoa. It is NOT first-line for uncomplicated strep throat—penicillin is preferred. It carries a risk of C. difficile colitis.
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) are for Gram-negative aerobes (e.g., Pseudomonas, Enterobacteriaceae). Gentamicin is dosed 5 mg/kg IV q24h (or extended-interval 5–7 mg/kg with trough monitoring); tobramycin is similar and anti-Pseudomonal; amikacin 15 mg/kg IV q24h for multi-drug resistant Gram-negatives. They require major dose reduction in renal failure and therapeutic drug monitoring; they are ototoxic and nephrotoxic. Gentamicin cannot be given without monitoring in stable CKD. Tobramycin is NOT effective against anaerobes. Amikacin is NOT safe in anuric patients—it requires dialysis removal.
Vancomycin (15–20 mg/kg IV q12h, adjusted to trough 15–20 µg/mL for serious infections) covers Gram-positives including MRSA and susceptible VRE. It does NOT cover Gram-negatives. It can cause nephrotoxicity and red man syndrome with rapid infusion.

## Aminoglycosides
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) are concentration-dependent antibiotics with a post-antibiotic effect. They are primarily active against aerobic Gram-negative bacteria, including Pseudomonas and Enterobacteriaceae. Dosing is typically once daily, with renal dose adjustment and therapeutic drug monitoring to avoid nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity.
Gentamicin is given at 5 mg/kg IV q24h, or extended-interval 5-7 mg/kg q24h with trough monitoring (trough <1 µg/mL). It requires major dose reduction in renal impairment. Tobramycin has similar dosing and is also anti-Pseudomonal. Amikacin is used for multi-drug resistant Gram-negative infections at 15 mg/kg IV q24h, with cautious use and monitoring.
Common exam traps: gentamicin is never given without monitoring in stable CKD; tobramycin is not effective against anaerobes; amikacin is not safe in anuric patients (it requires dialysis removal); and vancomycin does not cover Gram-negative bacteria. Vancomycin is a glycopeptide that covers Gram-positive organisms, including MRSA, and is dosed at 15-20 mg/kg IV q12h, adjusted to a trough of 15-20 µg/mL for serious infections.

## Glycopeptides
Glycopeptides like vancomycin and teicoplanin target Gram-positive bacteria, including MRSA and VRE. Vancomycin is dosed 15-20 mg/kg IV q12h, adjusted to a trough of 15-20 µg/mL for serious infections. Teicoplanin is given as a 400 mg IV/PO loading dose q12h, then q24h, and has a longer half-life. Both require renal adjustment: vancomycin needs CrCl calculation and trough monitoring, and teicoplanin must be adjusted in renal impairment.
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) cover aerobic Gram-negatives like Pseudomonas. Gentamicin is dosed 5 mg/kg IV q24h (or extended-interval 5-7 mg/kg with trough monitoring), with trough <1 µg/mL. Tobramycin is similar and anti-Pseudomonal. Amikacin is 15 mg/kg IV q24h for multi-drug resistant Gram-negatives. All require renal dose reduction and monitoring; they are not safe in anuric patients without dialysis removal, and they do not cover anaerobes.
Oxazolidinones (linezolid, tedizolid) are Gram-positive agents. Linezolid 600 mg PO/IV q12h can cause myelosuppression after 2-3 weeks and serotonin syndrome with SSRIs; monitor CBC even in renal failure. Tedizolid 200 mg once daily has less myelosuppression but still avoid concurrent serotonergic agents.
Co-trimoxazole (TMP-SMX) covers some Gram-positives and Gram-negatives (UTI, PCP), but not all community-acquired pneumonia due to limited streptococcal coverage. Metronidazole 500 mg PO/IV q8h covers anaerobes and protozoa, not aerobic Gram-negatives; no renal adjustment needed (hepatic metabolism).

## Oxazolidinones
Oxazolidinones (linezolid, tedizolid) cover Gram-positive bacteria like MRSA, VRE, and VSSA. Linezolid is dosed 600 mg PO/IV q12h; tedizolid is 200 mg PO/IV once daily. Both need no renal adjustment, but linezolid requires CBC monitoring because it can cause myelosuppression after 2-3 weeks, and tedizolid still requires avoiding serotonergic agents to prevent serotonin syndrome.
Teicoplanin (400 mg IV/PO q12h loading then q24h) has a similar spectrum but a longer half-life, so dosing is less frequent. Its dose must be adjusted in renal impairment—do not assume it is safe without adjustment.
Co-trimoxazole (TMP-SMX 160/800 mg PO/IV q12h) covers some Gram-positives (limited streptococci) and Gram-negatives (UTI, PCP). Reduce TMP dose if CrCl<30; SMX accumulates. It does not treat all community-acquired pneumonia.
Metronidazole (500 mg PO/IV q8h) targets anaerobes and protozoa (Giardia, C. difficile). It does not cover aerobic Gram-negatives. No renal adjustment is needed, but avoid alcohol and use cautiously in pregnancy.
